4.1.title: Therapeutic indications
4.1.text: Zeydovio is indicated for the treatment of adults with Short Bowel Syndrome (SBS). Patients should be stable following a period of intestinal adaptation after surgery.

4.2.title: Posology and method of administration
4.2.text:
Treatment should be initiated under the supervision of a medical professional with experience in the treatment of SBS.

Zeydovio treatment should not be initiated until it is reasonable to assume that the patient is stable following a period of intestinal adaptation and until the patient’s parenteral fluid and nutrition support is optimised. In addition, a colonoscopy of the entire colon and an upper gastro-intestinal endoscopy (or alternative imaging) with removal of polyps as appropriate (see section 4.4) should be performed prior to start of treatment.

Posology

Adults

The recommended dose of glepaglutide is 10 mg administered twice weekly.

Treatment effect should be evaluated after 6 months. If no overall improvement is achieved after these 6 months, it should be considered to switch to an alternative treatment or discontinue GLP-2 analogue treatment as a whole.

Continued treatment is recommended for patients who have weaned off parenteral nutrition.

Missed dose If a dose is missed, Zeydovio should be injected as soon as possible, and the next dose should be taken on the regularly scheduled day. Two doses must not be taken on the same day.

Monitoring of treatment Clinical assessment should consider individual treatment objectives and patient preferences. Efficacy and safety in all patients should be closely monitored on an ongoing basis according to clinical treatment guidelines. Patient’s weight and nutritional status should be closely monitored during treatment with glepaglutide to ensure appropriate nutritional support.

A follow-up colonoscopy and upper endoscopy (or alternative imaging) are recommended once a year during the first 2 years after starting treatment, and then at a minimum of 5-year intervals (see section 4.4).

Discontinuation of treatment Discontinuation of glepaglutide may result in fluid and electrolyte imbalance. It is recommended to monitor fluid and electrolyte status in patients who discontinue glepaglutide (see section 4.4). Glepaglutide treatment should be discontinued if no overall improvement of the patient condition is achieved.

Elderly No dose adjustment is necessary in patients above 65 years (see section 5.2).

Renal impairment No dose adjustment is necessary for patients with renal impairment (see section 5.2).

Hepatic impairment No dose adjustment is necessary for patients with mild and moderate hepatic impairment (limited data are available in patients with moderate hepatic impairment). No data are available in patients with severe hepatic impairment. Caution should be exercised if treating these patients with glepaglutide (see section 5.2).

Intestinal insufficiency No dose adjustment is necessary for patients achieving enteral autonomy during treatment with glepaglutide. Limited clinical data are available related to initiation of glepaglutide in SBS patients with intestinal insufficiency.

Paediatric population The safety and efficacy of glepaglutide in children and adolescents below 18 years of age have not yet been established. No data are available.

Method of administration

For subcutaneous use only.

Zeydovio should be administered twice weekly as a subcutaneous injection with an interval of 3-4 days between doses using the single-dose pre-filled pen.

Zeydovio is to be injected subcutaneously in the abdomen or thigh by using the pre-filled pen. It is recommended to alternate the injection sites within the chosen area of administration (thigh or abdomen).

For information on handling before administration, see section 6.6.

For instructions for use of the medicinal product, please refer to the ‘Instructions for Use’ at the end of the package leaflet.

4.3.title: Contraindications
4.3.text:
Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

Active or suspected malignancy.

Patients with a history of malignancies in the gastrointestinal tract, including the hepatobiliary system and pancreas within the last five years.

4.4.title: Special warnings and precautions for use
4.4.text:
Colorectal neoplasia A colonoscopy with removal of polyps should be performed at the time of starting treatment with glepaglutide. It is recommended to perform a colonoscopy once a year during the first 2 years after starting treatment, and then at a minimum of 5-year intervals. An individual assessment whether increased frequency of surveillance is necessary should be performed based on the patient characteristics and comorbidities. See also section 5.1. If a polyp is detected, adherence to current polyp follow-up guidelines is recommended. In case of malignancy, glepaglutide treatment must be discontinued (see section 4.3).

Gastric and small bowel neoplasia Gastric and small intestinal polyps have been reported in clinical studies with glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) analogues (see section 4.8). Therefore, upper gastro-intestinal endoscopy or other imaging is recommended at the time of starting treatment with glepaglutide, once a year during the first 2 years of treatment and then at a minimum of 5-year intervals. If a polyp is detected, it should be removed. In case of gastrointestinal malignancy, glepaglutide treatment must be discontinued (see section 4.3).

Intestinal stenosis and/or obstruction Intestinal stenosis and/or obstruction has been reported in clinical studies with glepaglutide (see section 4.8). In patients who develop intestinal stenosis and/or obstruction, temporarily discontinuation of glepaglutide is recommended. Glepaglutide may be restarted when the obstructive presentation resolves, if clinically indicated. In case of recurrent intestinal stenosis and/or stomal obstruction, the need for continued treatment with glepaglutide should be reassessed.

Gallbladder and biliary tract disease Cholecystitis, cholangitis (see section 4.8), and cholelithiasis have been reported in clinical studies with GLP-2 analogues. Monitoring of liver and gall bladder functions is recommended. If clinically meaningful changes are seen, further evaluation including imaging of the gallbladder and/or biliary tract is recommended and the need for continued glepaglutide treatment should be reassessed.

Pancreatic disease Pancreatitis has been reported in clinical studies with glepaglutide (see section 4.8). In case of pancreatitis, the need for continued treatment should be reassessed.

Fluid and electrolyte imbalance To avoid fluid overload or dehydration, careful adjustment of parenteral support is required in patients taking glepaglutide. Electrolyte balance and fluid status should be carefully monitored throughout treatment especially during initial treatment and after discontinuation of treatment.

Fluid overload has been reported in clinical studies with glepaglutide (see section 4.8). Patients, particularly those with cardiovascular disease (such as cardiac insufficiency and hypertension), should be monitored for fluid overload and advised to contact their physician in case of sudden weight gain, face swelling, swollen ankles, and/or dyspnoea. If clinically relevant fluid overload occurs, parenteral support should be adjusted.

Dehydration Patients with SBS are susceptible to dehydration that may lead to acute renal failure. In patients receiving glepaglutide, parenteral support should be reduced carefully and should not be discontinued abruptly. The patient’s fluid status should be evaluated following parenteral support reduction and corresponding adjustment performed, as needed.

Discontinuation of treatment Discontinuation of treatment with glepaglutide may result in fluid and electrolyte imbalance. It is recommended to monitor fluid and electrolyte status in patients who discontinue treatment with glepaglutide.

Concomitant medicinal products Patients receiving oral concomitant medicinal products requiring titration or with a narrow therapeutic index should be monitored closely due to potentially increased absorption (see section 4.5).

4.8.title: Undesirable effects
4.8.text:
Summary of the safety profile

The most commonly reported adverse reactions are in decreasing order injection site reactions (61%), gastrointestinal stoma complications (32.3%, based on patients with a stoma), abdominal pain (30.9%), nausea (22%), fluid retention/fluid overload (17.1%), vomiting (14.6%), and abdominal distension (12.2%).

Tabulated list of adverse reactions

Adverse reactions associated with glepaglutide obtained from three phase 3 clinical studies (two placebo-controlled parallel-arm studies and one open-label, single-arm study) are tabulated below. In these studies, 123 SBS patients, aged 18-82 years, were exposed to glepaglutide 10 mg once weekly or twice weekly for up to 4.5 years.

The adverse reactions are listed below by MedDRA system organ class and frequency category defined as: Very common (≥ 1/10); common (≥ 1/100 to < 1/10); uncommon (≥ 1/1 000 to < 1/100); rare (≥ 1/10 000 to < 1/1 000); very rare (< 1/10 000); not known (cannot be estimated from the available data). Within each frequency category, adverse reactions are presented in order of decreasing seriousness.

Description of selected adverse reactions

Hypersensitivity Adverse reactions such as hypersensitivity, injection site rash, injection site urticaria, and rash erythematous have been reported in 9.8% of patients in clinical studies with glepaglutide. Most reactions were mild, localised and of short duration. Three events were possibly suggestive of a generalised hypersensitivity reaction to glepaglutide, but none were indicative of anaphylaxis or SCAR (severe cutaneous adverse reaction).

Fluid retention/fluid overload Adverse reactions relate to fluid retention or fluid overload occurred in 17.1% of the patients in the clinical studies. These reactions included oedema peripheral, hypervolaemia, fluid retention, and generalised oedema.

Intestinal stenosis and/or obstruction Adverse reactions relating to intestinal stenosis and/or obstruction occurred in 8.9% of the patients. The events included intestinal obstruction, intestinal stenosis, small intestinal obstruction, and subileus.

Injection site reactions Injection site reactions were reported in 61 % of patients receiving glepaglutide. The reactions included symptoms like injection site induration, injection site bruising or heamatoma, injection site erythema, injection site pain, injection site paraesthesia, injection site swelling, injection site rash and injection site pruritus. The injection site reactions were generally mild.

Stoma complications Stoma complications were reported in 32.3 % of glepaglutide-treated patients with a stoma. In approximately 14% of events this led to surgical intervention. The most frequently reported stoma site complications was mild to moderate oedema/enlargement of the stoma nipple. Other stoma site complications include erythema, haemorrhage, ulceration, infection, irritation and pain.

Immunogenicity

Anti-drug antibodies (ADA) were detected in a total of 88 % of patients treated with glepaglutide. The ADA (incidence and titers) peaked after 12-24 weeks of treatment followed by a decreasing trend with continued glepaglutide treatment. Similarly, ADA cross-reacting with human GLP-2 found in 26 % of the patients were observed to disappear over time with continued glepaglutide treatment.

There was no identified clinically significant effect of ADA on pharmacokinetics, effectiveness, or safety of glepaglutide over the treatment duration of up to 4.5 years.

Reporting of suspected adverse reactions

Reporting suspected adverse reactions after authorisation of the medicinal product is important. It allows continued monitoring of the benefit/risk balance of the medicinal product. Healthcare professionals are asked to report any suspected adverse reactions via the national reporting system listed in Appendix V.

5.1.title: Pharmacodynamic properties
5.1.text:
Pharmacotherapeutic group: Other alimentary tract and metabolism products, various alimentary tract and metabolism products, ATC code: A16AX26

Mechanism of action

Glepaglutide is a long-acting analogue of GLP-2. Glepaglutide consists of 39 amino acids. When glepaglutide is injected subcutaneously, it forms a depot in the subcutaneous tissue, from which glepaglutide and its two main metabolites (both pharmacological active GLP-2 agonists) are released.

GLP-2 is a peptide secreted by L-cells predominantly located in the distal ileum and colon. GLP-2 possesses intestinotrophic properties and is known to increase intestinal and portal blood flow, inhibit

gastric acid secretion, and intestinal motility. In non-clinical studies, glepaglutide has been shown to promote growth leading to increased mucosal thickness and length of the intestine. In a clinical phase 2 study in SBS patients, glepaglutide showed increased intestinal epithelium height and crypt depth.

Pharmacodynamic effects

In functional in vitro assays, glepaglutide is a high-affinity GLP-2 receptor agonist, with receptor activity in the picomolar range. The agonistic activity of glepaglutide is supported by in vivo data showing a significant increase in small intestinal mass and length across various animal species and dosing regimens.

Based on the mechanism of action with the trophic effects on intestinal mucosa, there appears to be a risk for the promotion of small intestinal and/or colonic neoplasia (see section 4.4).

Intestinal absorption The ability of glepaglutide to improve intestinal absorption was studied in 18 adult patients with SBS (13 with intestinal failure and 5 with intestinal insufficiency) using daily doses of 0.1 mg, 1 mg, 10 mg (N=12 per dose group) in a 21-day, cross-over, double-blind, single-center, dose-ranging study.

From a second study (EASE-4), effect of glepaglutide on intestinal absorption was evaluated after 24 weeks of once-weekly dosing of glepaglutide 10 mg in 10 patients with SBS (8 with intestinal failure and 2 with intestinal insufficiency).

Both studies showed a clinically relevant increase in intestinal absorptive capacity (including wet weight absorption, energy and electrolytes) for the 1 mg once daily (OD), 10 mg OD and 10 mg once weekly (OW) doses. For EASE-4 wet weight absorption, the mean standard deviation (SD) change from baseline to week 24 was 398.4 (581.6) g/day and 1 037.7 (1 182.2) kJ/day for energy absorption. The intestinal absorptive capacity parameters were increased in a similar manner in both studies.

Intestinal epithelium Plasma citrulline levels, a biomarker of GLP-2 receptor activation and enterocyte mass were measured in EASE-1 study. A dose-dependent increase from baseline in plasma citrulline levels was observed for glepaglutide dose groups versus placebo after 24 weeks of treatment.

Cardiac electrophysiology At a dose 10 times the recommended dose, glepaglutide did not prolong the QT interval to any clinically relevant extent.

Clinical efficacy and safety

EASE-1 study The efficacy and safety of twice weekly (TW) or once weekly (OW) glepaglutide 10 mg was evaluated in a 24-week double blinded, randomised, multi-centre, placebo-controlled three arm study (EASE-1 study) in 106 SBS patients (randomised 1:1:1), dependent and stable on parenteral support (PS) and requiring PS at least 3 days per week.

The patient population had a mean age of 55 years (range 20 to 82 years), 25 patients were above 65 years, 4 patients were above 75 years, and 53.8 % were women. Stoma was present in 55 % (58/106) of the patients. The PS volume generally decreased over time in all three treatment groups showing a robust dose-response relationship with greater reductions achieved with more frequent glepaglutide dosing. For glepaglutide 10 mg TW there was a statistically significant reduction from baseline in PS volume compared to placebo after 24 weeks (Table 2 and Figure 1).

At week 24, a total of 9 patients were weaned off, 5 patients (14 %) in the TW group and 4 patients (11 %) in the OW group versus no patients in the placebo group.

The glepaglutide 10 mg OW dosing is not a recommended posology.

EASE-2 study Long-term clinical safety and efficacy are evaluated in 114 SBS patients (96 completers of EASE-1 study and 18 naive patients randomised directly into EASE-2 study).

The results from EASE-1 study were confirmed with a reduction in PS volume change from baseline of -5.4 L/week for glepaglutide 10 mg TW at 6 months. The reductions were sustained up to 2 years with a mean reduction in PS volume of 6.4 L/week in the 28 patients who have completed 2 years of treatment with glepaglutide 10 mg TW.

A reduction in PS ≥ 1 day/week was seen in 61.7 % of patients treated with glepaglutide 10 mg TW for 6 months, in 60.0 % after 12 months and in 67.9 % after 24 months.

A reduction from baseline of at least 20 % in weekly PS volume was found in 74.5 % of the patients, in 85.7 %, and in 92.9 % after 6, 12, and 24 months, respectively in the glepaglutide 10 mg TW treatment group.

Paediatric population

The European Medicines Agency has deferred the obligation to submit results of studies with Zeydovio in one or more subsets of the paediatric population in the treatment of short bowel syndrome (see section 4.2 for information on paediatric use).

5.2.title: Pharmacokinetic properties
5.2.text:
Absorption

After subcutaneous injection of glepaglutide the time to peak exposure ranged from 4-36 h and 4-24 h for OW and TW administration, respectively. Steady state is reached after 2-3 weeks of treatment with glepaglutide.

The peak exposure in SBS patients following long-term treatment with 10 mg glepaglutide TW for up to 4.5 years was 4 731 pmol/L (geometric mean of Cmax with range [1 755; 13 510]), whereas the maximum dose of 96 mg glepaglutide administered as a single dose in a healthy subject resulted in peak exposure of 73 677 pmol/L (geometric mean of Cmax with range: [42 934; 155 908]). Higher dose levels and exposures have not been investigated.

Glepaglutide is extensively metabolised in the subcutaneous depot, resulting in a low (0.5 %) absolute bioavailability of the parent drug after subcutaneous injection. Substantial amounts of the active metabolites M1 and M2 are released from the depot and, once steady state is reached, weekly cumulative exposure (AUC0-168h) to M1 and M2 exceeds that of the parent compound by 1.8-fold and 21-fold, respectively with TW dosing. This results in a considerably higher pharmacologically relevant bioavailability of glepaglutide compared to the absolute bioavailability of the parent compound.

The accumulation ratio for total glepaglutide is approximately1.7 with TW dosing. Anti-glepaglutide antibodies have a negligible effect on this ratio.

Distribution

Following intravenous injection, the parent drug has a volume of distribution (VSS) at steady state of 14.0 L. Similar low volumes of distribution following intravenous injections of the parent drug, M1 and M2 were seen indicating distribution to the extracellular space (based on animal data).

Biotransformation

After subcutaneous injection of glepaglutide, active metabolites are formed by carboxy terminal proteolytic degradation. Total glepaglutide covers parent, M1 and M2. All metabolites are potent GLP-2 agonists in vitro.

Glepaglutide, M1, and M2 are further metabolised into small peptides by catabolic pathways and these are further metabolised to free amino acids.

Elimination

The main route of elimination is via proteolytic metabolism.

The estimated effective half-life of glepaglutide 10 mg administered subcutaneously TW to SBS patients is approximately 70 hours.

Following IV dosing of healthy subjects, glepaglutide parent drug had a clearance of 5.72 L/h.

Linearity/non-linearity

In healthy participants, total exposure (AUC) to glepaglutide increased in a dose-proportional manner following single doses up to 24 mg and at steady state following once-weekly dosing over the range of 5 to 10 mg.

Pharmacokinetics in subpopulations

Based on observed data and population pharmacokinetic (PK) analysis age (studied range 18- 82 years), gender, body weight (studied range 42.4-107 kg), race, and renal impairment (mild, moderate, severe, impairment) do not have a clinically meaningful effect on the pharmacokinetics.

Renal impairment

In a phase 1 study, the effect of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of glepaglutide following subcutaneous administration of 10 mg glepaglutide was investigated. Severe renal impairment/end- stage renal disease had no clinically relevant impact on the pharmacokinetics of glepaglutide. See section 4.2.

Hepatic impairment

Based on population PK analysis, there is no clinically relvant change in the pharmacokinetics of glepaglutide in patients with mild hepatic impairment. Limited data are available in patients with moderate hepatic impairment. No data are available in patients with severe hepatic impairment. See section 4.2.

Drug-drug interactions

In vitro studies have shown no potential for glepaglutide to inhibit or induce CYP450 enzymes, and no potential to inhibit human drug transporter proteins.
